headline: NASA restates its 2028 Moon landing plan as China adds another state broadband batch
summary: NASA set out on 23 October how it intends to land astronauts on the Moon in 2028; Artemis III stays a crewed orbital test, with a summer 2027 launch in view and a two-day docking with a Blue Moon test lander.
China launched the 28th group of its state low-orbit internet satellites on a Long March 8A from Hainan on 25 October, fifteen days after the 27th.
Poland's prime minister closed his India visit in Bengaluru with space named as a priority, but no POLSA and ISRO agreement had been publicly reported.
Saudi Arabia's Royal Commission for AlUla commissioned two LaserSETI stations, the network's first site in Asia.

ESA's Council prepared a Europe-wide exploration proposal for the 15 December Rome meeting and approved two new directors; a Space Rider test model was lost over Sardinia, with the 2028 first flight still targeted.
Finland's ICEYE and Nokia signed a satcom letter of intent with Ukraine's defence ministry; Roscosmos's head said Russia and China are starting joint Mars hardware.
bottom_line: The weekend brought confirmation rather than new decisions: NASA kept its 2028 landing target and commercial landers at the centre of it, while China kept adding state broadband capacity. The next dated decisions are NASA's commercial station proposals on 8 December and ESA's Rome meeting on 15 December. In Europe, the week's moves were preparatory: ESA set the Rome agenda, and Ukraine expressed interest in, but did not order, a Finnish-built sovereign satcom system.

global.title: NASA restates a 2028 Moon landing and details the Artemis III orbital test
global.summary: NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman and agency leaders set out on 23 October the path to returning astronauts to the lunar surface in 2028. Artemis III will not land: it is a crewed mission in low Earth orbit, with officials pointing to a summer 2027 launch. Artemis programme manager Jeremy Parsons said the crew will dock with a Blue Moon lander test article for two days to check life support and other systems. Isaacman had told staff in a September memo that Artemis III was about three months behind schedule, and Bloomberg reports concern that hardware may not be ready in time. Lunar terrain vehicles for later surface operations are to come from Lunar Outpost and Venturi Astrolab.
global.why: The briefing confirmed the restructured sequence rather than changing it: an orbital test in 2027 and a landing attempt in 2028. It follows the 23 October ledger entry that flagged the update, and keeps commercial landers, not SLS alone, at the centre of the schedule.

global.title: China launches the 28th batch of its state low-orbit internet constellation
global.summary: A Long March 8A lifted off from the Hainan commercial spacecraft launch site at 10:03 Beijing time on 25 October and placed the 28th group of low-orbit internet satellites in orbit, according to Xinhua. The satellites were built by the China Academy of Space Technology. The state announcement gave the group number but not the number of spacecraft. The 27th group flew on a Long March 12 from the same site on 10 October. The Long March 8A is designed for constellation launches to medium and low Earth orbit.
global.why: Two state broadband batches in fifteen days show a steady deployment cadence for the state-backed network. It is the Chinese counterpart to the sovereign connectivity question raised by the Starlink dispute in Ukraine recorded in the ledger.

items.title: ESA Council readies Rome exploration package and names two directors
items.summary: The 350th ESA Council met at delegate level in Paris on 21 and 22 October. Member States discussed the Director General's proposal 'Europe's Future in Space Exploration', which sets out a scalable path in low Earth orbit, on the Moon and towards Mars, and advanced preparations for the Intermediate Ministerial Meeting in Rome on 15 December. ESA describes IMM26 as a step towards programme and financial decisions at CM28, while allowing early preparatory work within existing budgets. Delegates also reviewed ESA-EU relations, including the next EU Multiannual Financial Framework, the European Competitiveness Fund, the EU Space Act and the EUSPA regulation; ESA called for a clear division of responsibilities without duplication. The Council approved Andrzej Banasiak as Director of Commercialisation and Industry Partnership and Nicolaus Hanowski as Director of Space Operations, both from 1 January 2027.
items.why: The Council fixed the agenda for Rome rather than taking funding decisions, and confirmed two senior appointments. It moves the 15 December IMM26 entry from a date to a defined exploration proposal.

items.title: Tusk's Bengaluru stop closes without a published POLSA and ISRO agreement
items.summary: Prime Minister Donald Tusk visited Bengaluru on 23 October with a business delegation of about 100, including the Polish Space Agency and ICEYE. Defence24 reports that both sides named space as an area with strong potential and that more than a dozen MoUs were signed at business forums in Delhi and Bengaluru. The two prime ministers set a goal of doubling bilateral trade to USD 12 billion by 2030. A POLSA and ISRO cooperation agreement had been trailed before the visit, but no signing had been publicly reported at the time of publication. Space24 notes that ICEYE set up an Indian subsidiary in August and cites reports that it is discussing a sovereign radar constellation for India.
items.why: The visit ended with political backing for space cooperation but no confirmed agency-level text. It updates the 23 October ledger entry, which listed the POLSA and ISRO agreement as planned.

items.title: Finnish firms ICEYE and Nokia sign satcom letter of intent with Ukraine's defence ministry
items.summary: ICEYE and Nokia signed a Letter of Intent with Ukraine's Ministry of Defence on 22 October to explore cooperation on sovereign satellite communications. It was announced during Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo's visit to Kyiv, where President Volodymyr Zelensky said seven agreements worth about EUR 300 million were concluded. The letter builds on the companies' 1 October partnership to offer government-owned LEO broadband systems, with nations controlling satellites, ground segment and terminals. An ICEYE spokesperson told Breaking Defense that the letter is an expression of intent and does not imply an order. No value or timetable has been attributed to the satcom element.
items.why: It is the first government expression of interest in the ICEYE-Nokia sovereign satcom offer, and it came inside a Finnish state visit. It follows reported throttling of Starlink service in Ukraine earlier this month.

items.title: Space Rider test model lost over Sardinia; ESA keeps 2028 maiden flight
items.summary: ESA's Director of Space Transportation, Géraldine Naja, told a briefing on 22 October that a full-scale Space Rider test model was lost in a drop test on 6 October. The model was released from a helicopter at about three kilometres over a military range in Sardinia; the drogue parachute deployed, but the parafoil detached and the model struck the ground. Remnants were recovered and an investigation board has been set up. Naja said the remaining qualification work is not on the programme's critical path, but that the schedule will be reviewed once the board reports. ESA still targets the first half of 2028 for the first flight on Vega C.
items.why: This is the first failure at system level in Space Rider's landing test campaign, which runs from an Italian range. The 2028 target stands for now, subject to the investigation.

items.title: Roscosmos head says Russia and China are starting work on joint Mars hardware
items.summary: Roscosmos Director General Dmitry Bakanov said on 21 October, after taking part in the Russia-China heads-of-government meeting in St Petersburg, that the two countries are beginning a joint Mars mission, starting with building instruments and equipment. State agency RIA Novosti, quoting Roscosmos, reported that he cited the joint Chang'e-7 lunar mission as the existing precedent (translated from Russian by ATLAS). He called China one of Russia's key partners and said the two countries exchange Earth observation data and jointly use GLONASS and BeiDou navigation signals. No mission name, timeline, budget or signed agreement was published. Both outlets carrying the statement are state media.
items.why: A named top official has put a Russia-China Mars effort on record for the first time in this cycle, though without a published agreement. It sits alongside existing Russian instruments on China's Chang'e-7 lunar mission.

sources.title: AlUla Announces Commissioning of Two LaserSETI Astronomical Observation Stations at Project's First Site in Asia
SETI Institute and Royal Commission for AlUla Bring Two LaserSETI Stations to Saudi Arabia

items.title: Royal Commission for AlUla commissions two LaserSETI stations
items.summary: The Royal Commission for AlUla announced on 25 October that two LaserSETI stations at AlUla Manara are installed and commissioned. The SETI Institute says the stations were installed on 19 August, are fully operational, and are the network's first site in Asia. The institute will run and maintain them for three years with the commission under a partnership announced in August 2024. The stations monitor the night sky for transient optical events. The state agency framed the step as part of Vision 2030.
items.why: A state body is building ground-based astronomy capacity alongside the Saudi Space Agency's programmes. It is a new ledger entry for Saudi Arabia; the scale is small and the work is scientific rather than industrial.

audio_sections.title: Opening
audio_sections.text:
Good morning. It's Monday, the twenty sixth of October, and here's what's happening in space.

NASA has laid out how it plans to get astronauts back on the Moon in twenty twenty eight. China has added another batch of satellites to its state internet network. And Poland's prime minister has wrapped up his visit to India, with space high on the agenda but no new agency deal on paper. Closer to home, Europe's space agency has set its agenda for a December meeting in Rome, and Finland's ICEYE and Nokia have signed a satellite deal with Ukraine.

audio_sections.title: Top story
audio_sections.text:
The top story comes from Florida. On Friday, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman and senior agency leaders gave an update on the Artemis programme at Kennedy Space Center.

The headline is that the plan hasn't changed. NASA still aims to land astronauts on the Moon in twenty twenty eight. Before that, Artemis three will fly as a crewed test in low Earth orbit, rather than going to the Moon, and officials pointed to a launch in the summer of twenty twenty seven.

The programme manager, Jeremy Parsons, explained what the crew will actually do. They'll dock with a test version of Blue Origin's Blue Moon lander and stay attached for two days, climbing inside to check life support and other key systems. It's a rehearsal for the hardware that will eventually carry people down to the surface.

There are question marks over timing, though. Isaacman told NASA staff in a memo last month that Artemis three was running about three months behind, and Bloomberg reports concern that some hardware may not be ready in time. NASA's answer, for now, is that the schedule holds.

The bigger picture is that commercial landers, not just NASA's own rocket, now set the pace for the whole programme.

audio_sections.title: Around the world
audio_sections.text:
In China, a Long March eight A rocket lifted off from the commercial launch site on Hainan island on Sunday morning, Beijing time. According to the state news agency Xinhua, it carried the twenty eighth group of satellites for China's low orbit internet network, built by the China Academy of Space Technology.

The official notice didn't say how many satellites were on board, only the group number. The previous batch went up just fifteen days earlier. Put simply, China is building a national broadband network in orbit, batch by batch, at a steady clip. For governments weighing up where their satellite connections come from, that's now a second network of this scale taking shape, alongside SpaceX's Starlink.

In Saudi Arabia, the Royal Commission for AlUla says two LaserSETI stations are now up and running at its AlUla Manara observatory site. They watch the night sky for brief flashes of light, and the SETI Institute says they're the network's first stations anywhere in Asia. It's a small, scientific step, but it shows Saudi institutions building research capacity on the ground, as well as in orbit.

audio_sections.title: Closer to home
audio_sections.text:
In Poland, Prime Minister Donald Tusk finished his India trip in Bengaluru on Friday. He travelled with about a hundred business leaders, including the Polish Space Agency and the radar satellite company ICEYE.

Both governments said space has strong potential, and more than a dozen agreements were signed between companies at business forums in Delhi and Bengaluru. The two prime ministers also set a goal of doubling trade to twelve billion dollars by twenty thirty.

What hasn't appeared, at least not publicly, is the cooperation agreement between the Polish Space Agency and India's space agency, ISRO, which had been talked about before the trip. So the political backing is there, but the formal framework is still to come.

Polish coverage has focused on the openings for Polish space companies. The specialist site Space24 points out that ICEYE set up an Indian subsidiary in August, and cites reports that it's discussing a radar satellite constellation for India.

audio_sections.title: Europe and Eurasia
audio_sections.text:
Now to Europe. The European Space Agency's member states met in Paris on Wednesday and Thursday to prepare for a ministers' meeting in Rome on the fifteenth of December. On the table is a proposal called Europe's Future in Space Exploration, a step by step path in low Earth orbit, on the Moon and towards Mars.

In Western Europe, ESA confirmed that a full size Space Rider test model was lost over a military range in Sardinia on the sixth of October, when its main parafoil came away. ESA is still aiming for a first flight in the first half of twenty twenty eight.

In the Nordics, Finland's ICEYE and Nokia signed a letter of intent with Ukraine's defence ministry on Thursday, during the Finnish prime minister's Kyiv visit, to explore a satellite network Ukraine would own and control. ICEYE stresses it's not an order, and no price or timetable has been given.

In Russia, the head of Roscosmos, Dmitry Bakanov, said Russia and China are starting work on instruments for a joint Mars mission. The remarks were carried by state media, and no agreement or timeline has been published.

audio_sections.title: Industry and markets
audio_sections.text: On the business side, SpaceX has told US regulators it ended the third quarter with more than eleven thousand one hundred Starlink satellites in orbit, and that it added one point six million customers over those three months. Analysts quoted by CNBC say that, for governments looking for an alternative, there's still no ready replacement. That's the backdrop to Ukraine's recent move to explore a satellite network of its own.

audio_sections.title: The days ahead
audio_sections.text: Looking ahead, the Asia Pacific regional space agency forum opens in Bangkok tomorrow, and the Defence in Space conference begins in London. On Thursday, astronauts on the space station start the first of two spacewalks to fit new solar arrays. The European Parliament's industry committee votes on the EU Space Act on the tenth of November. NASA's commercial space station proposals are due on the eighth of December, and ESA ministers meet in Rome on the fifteenth.

audio_sections.title: Close
audio_sections.text: That's the briefing for today. You'll find the full edition, with links to every source, on the Briefing tab. Have a good day.
